methodological_questions: How is portability defined and measured for players who change teams?
Is n=24 enough to detect a cut-vs-drive difference in portability?
Is the cut-heavy/drive-heavy classification measured before the move and independent of the outcome?
How should regression to the mean, teammate and context change, and minutes change be handled?
Do findings for connectors carry over to shapers?

historical_evidence.finding: For connector movers (n=92), pre-move cut share was positively associated with the portability delta (Spearman rho=+0.265, p=0.011, AUC 0.653). Cut-minus-drive share gave rho=+0.314, p=0.002, AUC 0.656. Drive share gave rho=-0.278, p=0.007. The top cut tercile was 65% portable (median delta +0.167) against a median of -0.039 for the bottom group. Leave-one-out AUC was 0.622 and the permutation p was 0.005. The record lists sensitivity checks (drop Gafford / top-3, position splits) but the retrieved text does not give their results. The record is flagged LIM:small_sample / RISK:SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER.

Connector diet x destination structural-gap match. The connector subsets (n=19 and 40) were too small: match vs mismatch delta +0.540 vs +0.069, p=0.156 (n=5/14). The all-movers binary delta p=0.0283 did not replicate as a continuous Spearman (-0.034) and was not the licensed connector test.

DRIVE-as-BEST counter vs a constrained mix (n=44). The observed gap (-0.066 PPP) was below the minimum detectable effect of 0.180 PPP at 80% power. The data could not distinguish a true null from an effect up to about 0.18 PPP.
Destination net-rating checks for movers were described as 'underpowered and null once corrected for landing-spot quality' (no numbers recorded). The check was dropped from Paper 1.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Subgroup tests on small connector subsets (n=19/40), and an all-movers binary test used as a stand-in for the connector test
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as LIM:small_sample / RISK:SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER. The all-movers binary result did not replicate as a continuous association.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Testing a PPP effect at n=44 against a feasibility-constrained baseline
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as LIM:low_power_large_MDE and LIM:small_sample. The MDE of 0.18 PPP exceeded the observed gap.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Using destination on-court net rating change as the portability outcome
failed_approaches.why: Recorded as underpowered and null after correction for landing-spot quality (LIM:low_power_large_MDE, LIM:small_sample).

evidence_establishes: For connector movers (n=92), pre-move cut share was positively associated, and drive share negatively associated, with a portability delta (FAM:SF-CHT-057, status supported). The direction matches the present hypothesis.
Small subgroup tests (n of about 19 to 44) and net-rating outcomes have repeatedly been recorded as untestable or underpowered in this project (FAM:SF-APPS-090, FAM:SF-APPS-024, FAM:SF-PAP-029).
evidence_does_not_establish: That the cut > drive portability relationship holds for the 'shaper' role. The supported record is about connectors, and the retrieved records do not say how shapers relate to connectors.
That n=24 movers can detect an effect of the size seen in connectors. No power analysis for n=24 was retrieved.
That the effect survives out of sample on 2025-26 data. The retrieved text does not say whether FAM:SF-CHT-057 used any holdout.
That net-rating or outcome-based portability follows the same pattern. FAM:SF-PAP-029 suggests outcome-based checks are null or underpowered.
own_inferences: The cut-heavy vs drive-heavy contrast is partly mechanical. Cut share and drive share are components of one mix, so the rho for cut share and the rho for drive share in FAM:SF-CHT-057 are not independent confirmations. The cut-minus-drive contrast is the single natural primary test.

With n=24 and an effect like the connector one (rho about 0.27 to 0.31), two-sided power at alpha=0.05 is roughly 0.2 to 0.3 by Fisher-z approximation. About 80% power would need |rho| of roughly 0.55. A null at n=24 would therefore be uninformative, and a significant result would likely be an inflated estimate.

A fair reading of the question is a replication or extension of FAM:SF-CHT-057 in a different taxonomy class. It is informative only as an estimate with a confidence interval, or pooled with connector evidence if the role definitions are compatible.

The 'portable' label depends on a delta that may be partly derived from the same play-type records used to compute cut and drive share. That creates outcome-derived-label and regression-to-the-mean risks. High pre-move cut share may also mean a specific team scheme, which would confound the result.
uncertainties: How 'shaper' is defined and how it differs from 'connector'; the 24 units may overlap with the 92 connector movers.
How 'travel', 'portability' and 'cut-heavy' are operationalised, including the delta formula and the thresholds.
Whether the n=24 units are movers only, and whether they include 2025-26 movers.
Whether the n=24 is complete or partial for 2025-26. The regular season is complete from 2026-04-13 and the playoffs from 2026-06-21.
The results of the sensitivity checks in FAM:SF-CHT-057 (the retrieved text is truncated).
Whether the pre-move and post-move sample sizes (possessions or minutes) are enough to measure shares reliably.

historical_effect.explanation: Without history I would have been undecided between proceeding and not proceeding. FAM:SF-CHT-057 (supported) gives a prior for the sign and rough size of the effect and a ready measurement framework, which favours running a narrowly specified test. The untestable records (FAM:SF-APPS-090, FAM:SF-APPS-024, FAM:SF-PAP-029) show that small n and outcome-based endpoints repeatedly fail in this project. This moved the decision to proceed_with_changes: one pre-registered primary test with interval estimation, no subgroup fishing, no net-rating endpoint, and no confirmatory claim from n=24 alone.

blocking_constraints.text: n=24 gives roughly 0.2 to 0.3 power for rho about 0.3, and about 80% power only for |rho| of about 0.55 or more. A null cannot be interpreted as rejection.
Cut and drive shares from limited per-player possessions may be noisy, which attenuates the association. The 'shaper' label and the portability delta need explicit reliability checks.

prior_work.summary: FAM:SF-CHT-057 (supported) found that cut share predicts portability for connector movers (n=92). The retrieved records do not show the same test for shapers. The other three records are untestable results from small n or outcome-based endpoints and are cautionary rather than answers.

risks.text: n=24 is far below what the prior effect size needs. Any significant result will probably overstate the effect (winner's curse), and a null will be inconclusive.
If the portability delta and the cut/drive shares both come from the same play-type possession records, shared measurement error or overlap can create association.
Players with extreme pre-move shares or extreme pre-move organizational function will regress toward the mean after moving, which can mimic or hide a portability difference.
Destination team, coach scheme, teammate quality, minutes and usage changes, and player position (bigs cut more) are all linked to both cut share and portability.
Per-player share estimates may be unreliable with few possessions. The derived play-type records depend on the play-by-play parser.
The prior record reports several correlated metrics (cut share, cut-minus-drive, drive share, AUC, terciles). Choosing among them after the fact would inflate false positives.
Pre-move shares must come only from games before the move. Role classification using full-season data that includes post-move games would leak.
The 2022-23 to 2025-26 seasons may differ in league play-type mix and rules. 2025-26 playoff data is partial before 2026-06-21.
If most shapers are portable or most are not, tercile hit rates and AUC are hard to interpret without the base rate.

design.estimand: Spearman correlation, within shaper movers, between pre-move cut-minus-drive share (cuts / (cuts + drives) among role-relevant actions) and the portability delta, defined as the change in the shaper's organizational-function measure from the last pre-move season to the first post-move season, using the FAM:SF-CHT-057 definitions where compatible. The hypothesis is directional: rho>0. Secondary: a binary 'portable' indicator and AUC, reported with bootstrap CIs.
design.unit: Shaper who changed teams between consecutive observed seasons (2022-23 to 2025-26), one row per move (n=24). A player with multiple moves gets one row for the first move, or is handled with a cluster bootstrap.
design.sample: The 24 stated units. Require minimum pre-move and post-move possession or minute counts fixed before analysis (suggest at least 200 pre-move and 200 post-move involved actions). Lock the data version and the shaper and portability definitions before looking at outcomes. Do not alter the sample after seeing results.
design.power: Fisher-z calculation at n=24: two-sided alpha=0.05 power is about 0.2 to 0.3 for rho of 0.27 to 0.31, and 80% power needs |rho| of about 0.55 or more. The study is therefore exploratory or estimation-focused. Report the point estimate with a 95% bootstrap CI and compare it to the FAM:SF-CHT-057 estimate (rho about 0.27 to 0.31). Do not claim confirmation or rejection unless the CI is narrow enough to exclude, or include, the connector-sized effect.
design.controls: Partial Spearman or a small regression adjusting for pre-move portability baseline (to address regression to the mean), position group, pre- and post-move minutes change and sample size, and destination team structural-gap measures. Compute shares only from pre-move games (no lookahead). Check how well the shares split-half reproduce before the move. Fit the model with few covariates, because of n=24.
design.falsification: (1) Permutation test with 5000 label shuffles for the primary rho. (2) Placebo: use pre-move cut share to predict a non-role outcome such as minutes change, and also a placebo 'move' in non-mover seasons. (3) Leave-one-out and drop-top-3 influence checks. (4) Replicate on the connector movers in FAM:SF-CHT-057 as a method check only, and treat connector-to-shaper agreement as supporting but not independent evidence. (5) Do not use destination net rating as the outcome, per FAM:SF-PAP-029.
design.multiplicity: One primary test (directional rho for cut-minus-drive share vs portability delta at alpha=0.05). Everything else (AUC, terciles, cut share alone, drive share alone, position splits) is labelled exploratory with no p-value claims, or is corrected by Holm if reported as inferential.
design.decision_rule: Supported (tentatively): primary rho>0, permutation p<0.05, the 95% CI excludes 0, the sign survives leave-one-out and the covariate-adjusted version. Rejected: only if the CI excludes connector-sized effects (upper bound of rho below about 0.2), which is unlikely at n=24. Otherwise label inconclusive or untestable at this n. Treat any claim as hypothesis-generating until replicated on additional movers, for example 2026-27 data.
design.data_version: NBA per-game files and derived play-type possession records for 2022-23 through 2025-26 (regular season and playoffs). Fix the data snapshot, parser version and shaper/portability definitions before analysis. Only the complete 2025-26 regular season (from 2026-04-13) and playoffs (from 2026-06-21) are used.

methodological_questions: How is role transfer or portability measured when players change teams?
Is n=24 units enough to detect a difference in role stability between cut-heavy and drive-heavy shapers?
How are cut-heavy and drive-heavy shapers classified, and is the classification reliable and independent of the outcome?
How should regression to the mean, teammate and context changes, and minutes changes be handled in role-persistence comparisons?
args.query: Do cut-heavy shaper roles persist across team changes better than drive-heavy shaper roles? Prior studies of role portability, role stability, shaper classification and small-sample limits.

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): n=24

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm weighing whether a cut-heavy shaper role travels better than a drive-heavy one, using 24 units. The earlier finding on connectors, where cut share predicted portability, may not carry over, since I'm not sure shapers are coded under the same role taxonomy.

I'm checking whether the connector finding even carries over to shapers, since they may sit under a different role taxonomy. With only 24 units, power to detect an effect of the size seen before is very low, so a test here would likely be inconclusive. Cut and drive shares are also mechanically linked, so they aren't independent evidence.

I'm settling on proceed_with_changes as a single pre-specified test, using Spearman correlation between pre-move cut-minus-drive share and portability delta among shaper movers, with CI reporting and an informative prior drawn from the connector effect. Power at n=24 is only about 0.3 for a rho near 0.3, so I'd flag this as unlikely to be confirmatory, with high odds of an uncertain result.
